boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Cabin Creek record (July 1-2, 1863) in Operations to Control Indian Territory [June-September 1863]. The train's march from Baxter Springs, the Greenleaf Prairie fight and Cabell's failure to cross Grand River are context. Campaign-wide marches, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Detachments from nine units [US] and two regiments and detachments from two other units (approx. 1,600-1,800) [CS]; the frozen CS bounds are both 1,600. The live field reads 1500 (US 0; CS 1500), while the live description gives Watie about 1,600 to 1,800 and Cabell about 1,500 reinforcements. Williams says prisoners put the enemy at 1,600 to 1,800, naming Watie's and McIntosh's regiments and 600 men of two Texas regiments (a compiler's note says the Twenty-seventh Texas was then in Mississippi), and that his attacking column was less than 900 men. Britton gives Watie about sixteen hundred, Cabell about fifteen hundred with three guns (unable to cross), and Foreman's reinforcement of six hundred mounted men.
claims.rationale: A prisoners' estimate, an attacking-column figure and a history's figures; the frozen upper bound does not match its own text. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live US zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Williams says the enemy was strongly posted on Cabin Creek commanding the ford, concealed behind logs in thick brush, and that the creek, swollen by rain, was too high to cross the train on July 1; his infantry waded to the armpits the next morning. Britton says a line of rifle-pits on the south bank was covered with willow boughs so it could not be seen from the north bank. NPS says high water on Grand River detained Cabell and on Cabin Creek prevented a crossing at first.
claims.rationale: Ground and water from an interested report, a history and a summary; the concealed works predate the attack, but their exact timing is not established.

claims.value: The action was fought to pass a supply train to Fort Gibson. Britton says Phillips's command was on short rations and then a diet of fresh beef, salt, rice and wheat before the train arrived, and that the train was corralled on the prairie a mile or so back from the ford; Williams puts it about 2 miles from the ford. NPS says the train delivered its supplies to Fort Gibson.
claims.rationale: Train movements from an interested report, a history and a summary; no quartermaster record inspected.

claims.value: Williams says it was known that a large force had been concentrated to attack the train, and he took the enemy's strength from prisoners. Britton says prisoners taken by Parsons's Cherokees gave Watie's position and strength and Cabell's inability to cross, and that Indian women had earlier brought word of Cabell to Fort Gibson. NPS says Williams learned Watie intended to attack him at the crossing.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 88 total (US 23; CS 65); the live field reads 80 (US 21; CS 59). Williams gives his loss as 1 killed and about 20 wounded, and estimates the enemy's at not less than 50 killed, as many wounded and 9 prisoners. Britton gives the official Federal loss as three killed and thirty wounded, and Williams's Confederate estimate as about fifty killed and nine prisoners.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Williams's Confederate figures are an estimate.

open_questions: Phillips's report (No. 1, read in part and not selected) and Foreman's report (No. 3), any Confederate report of Watie or Wells, and the return of casualties mentioned by Phillips remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Wiley Britton's The Civil War on the Border, volume II (Putnam's, 1899) is a retrospective history described on its title page as based upon official reports and the author's observations; it relays figures from Union and Confederate reports, so it is not independent of the Official Records families, and is treated as partly a participant's interested Union account. Williams's July 1863 report on Cabin Creek, Cooper's August 12, 1863 report on Elk Creek (Honey Springs) and Cabell's December 7, 1863 report including Backbone Mountain are separate author families of interested accounts; Cooper's inclosed general orders are part of his report. Official Records Series I, Volume XXII, Part 1 is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
